factor_scores.evidence_summary: Lombard's public audit directory lists multiple 2026 engagements but expressly says some contracts changed after audit. The published material does not map every active deployed implementation to an audited commit, so audit-scope matching cannot be established green; no material mismatch is publicly verified. Yellow.

The official EVM audit directory lists a 2026-07-07 OpenZeppelin Mint Limits review covering BaseLBTC, BridgeTokenAdapter, NativeLBTC, StakedLBTC, and RateLimitsV2—17 days before this assessment. Its listed scope is recent deployed-security-critical functionality, meeting the recency threshold. Green.

OZ V2 audit (Nov-Dec 2024): 39 total findings, 32 resolved, 3 partially resolved. Two high-severity findings remain partially resolved: (1) Sanctioned Address Checks — bridge and unstake strategies lacked sanction checks, team deferred full implementation pending future economic incentive mechanisms; (2) Unstake Payment Reuse — single BTC tx could satisfy multiple unstake payloads, team deferred fix. Both partially-resolved highs relate to the Golang Lombard Ledger layer (not EVM smart contracts directly). All OZ V2 EVM-layer findings appear resolved. Veridise V1 and V2: 0 findings each, so no unverifiable resolutions there. Halborn V1/V1.5/V2 reports not individually reviewed for resolution status but no post-audit finding regression reported in subsequent audits.

The official EVM audit directory lists publicly accessible work by at least five independent firms—Halborn, Veridise, OpenZeppelin, Sherlock, and ABDK—across core, bridge, yield, strategy, and mint-limit modules. This is well above the multi-firm threshold. Green.

OpenZeppelin is a confirmed Tier-1 audit firm (on the enumerated Tier-1 list per methodology). Lombard has 5 OZ engagements spanning 2024-2026 covering EVM contracts including the most recent multipauser audit (April 2026). Veridise, Halborn, Sherlock, and ABDK are established Tier-2 firms with public track records and indexed audit histories. Green threshold: at least one Tier-1 audit of deployed code — confirmed via OZ.

Most recent audit-to-deploy gap: Sherlock multipauser sign-off 2026-04-01, OZ multipauser sign-off 2026-04-09, on-chain upgrade 2026-04-24. Gaps of 23 days (Sherlock) and 15 days (OZ) — both well within the ≤60-day green threshold. All other audits in the history also appear to have been deployed within the green window given the active development cadence and close audit follow-up timing.

Immunefi lists an active, triaged Lombard program since 2024-09-04, updated 2026-07-15, with a $250,000 maximum smart-contract reward and 53 assets in scope. The $250,000 maximum remains below the $500,000 green threshold, so yellow.

The reviewed public Lombard transparency and Immunefi materials establish a current disclosure channel, but they do not establish whether any prior vulnerability report was ignored before an exploit. No public incident/disclosure record supporting either conclusion was located. Gray rather than inferring a clean history from absence of evidence.

No formal verification (Certora Prover, Kani, Halmos, or equivalent) has been performed on any Lombard EVM contracts. None of the 12+ audit reports in the GitHub directory reference formal verification. Veridise audits use static analysis and manual code review, not FV. OZ audits use Slither-family tooling and manual review. No Certora specification files found in the evm-smart-contracts repository. Per methodology: red = 0% formal verification coverage. No critical invariants formally specified or proved.

No published Slither/Mythril/Semgrep run output exists for Lombard EVM contracts. Using published audit findings as proxy. Veridise V1 (0 findings), Veridise V2 (0 findings), OZ V2 (8 high across both Golang and EVM layers, 6 fully resolved, 2 partially resolved — but partially-resolved items are Golang/Ledger layer, not EVM). The Ackee Solana audit found 1 high ('Possible unauthorized LBTC minting') — acknowledged/fixed per audit summary. No active unresolved high-severity EVM finding identified from published audits. Cannot definitively count Slither findings without a tool run — scored yellow because audit evidence is secondary proxy.

No published Slither suicidal detector output available. Local tool run not performed per dry-run methodology. Factory directory exists in repo (CREATE3-based deployment) but factory source was not retrieved. Post-Cancun EIP-6780 limits SELFDESTRUCT to same-transaction deployments, reducing risk, but deployed contracts target Paris EVM version (pre-Cancun behavior applies to legacy deployments). No audit finding flags SELFDESTRUCT in non-admin paths. Marked gray — needs tool run.

No delegatecall with user-controlled target found in examined contracts. TransparentUpgradeableProxy uses delegatecall internally but target is admin-controlled (ProxyAdmin / TimelockController). Consortium.sol: no delegatecall. BridgeV2.sol: no delegatecall found. NativeLBTC.sol: standard ERC-20 operations, no delegatecall. Full repository scan was not performed — confidence medium because peripheral contracts (PMM, StakeAndBake, GMP) were not exhaustively reviewed.

No arbitrary call with user-controlled target found in examined contracts. BridgeV2.sol routes calls through defined interfaces (Hyperlane Mailbox, CCIP Router) which are admin-configured trusted addresses, not user-supplied. The GMP/AssetRouter integration uses a defined Mailbox address (0x964677F337d6528d659b1892D0045B8B27183fc0). No evidence of fully user-controlled call target. Confidence medium — peripheral contracts not fully inspected.

BridgeV2.sol imports ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable and applies the nonReentrant modifier to deposit() (multiple overloads) and handlePayload() — the most external-call-heavy functions. BaseLBTC.sol also inherits ReentrancyGuardUpgradeable. Core bridge and minting functions are guarded. No reentrancy finding in any published audit (Veridise 0 findings; OZ findings were governance/logic, not reentrancy). Peripheral contracts (PMM, StakeAndBake, iDepositor) not fully inspected.

LBTC is an ERC-20 token (8 decimals). No ERC-777, ERC-1155, or ERC-721 integration detected in core token contracts. StakeAndBake/iDepositor may interact with NFT staking position tokens for Babylon integration but no evidence of unguarded callback paths in EVM contracts. No audit finding flags this pattern.

No published Slither divide-before-multiply detector output available. Tool run not performed. LBTC uses 8 decimals (BTC-matched) creating potential mixed-decimal arithmetic with 18-decimal EVM ecosystem tokens. Veridise V2 found 0 findings (suggests no divide-before-multiply in scope), but the exact Slither output is not published. Marked gray — needs tool run.

LBTC uses 8 decimals; most EVM DeFi integrations use 18 decimals. Cross-decimal arithmetic risk exists in StakeAndBake, iDepositor, and PMM contracts where LBTC interacts with 18-decimal tokens. No published audit flags this as unresolved in the EVM layer. Cannot confirm safe normalization without source inspection of all arithmetic paths. Marked gray — needs curator review of cross-decimal math paths.
No independently verifiable public static-analysis, symbolic-execution, or audit evidence establishes whether deployed Lombard contracts contain signed/unsigned arithmetic confusion.
factor_scores.notes: Not assessed: the available public materials do not provide a tool result or sufficiently complete deployed-code assessment for this factor; no local tool run is permitted in this refresh pass.

factor_scores.evidence_summary: GitHub search for 'ecrecover' in evm-smart-contracts returns 0 results — no direct ecrecover calls in the codebase. Consortium.sol uses OpenZeppelin ECDSA.tryRecover() which handles zero-address returns internally and is a safe wrapper. BridgeV2.sol uses no ecrecover. No raw ecrecover call exists to create a zero-address bypass risk.

NativeLBTC and StakedLBTC inherit from BaseLBTC which uses OZ's ERC20PermitUpgradeable (EIP-2612). OZ's EIP-712 implementation includes chainId in the domain separator by default. No cross-chain replay risk from missing chainId in domain separator as OZ 5.0.2 always includes chainId. Cross-chain message replay for bridge operations is handled at the BridgeV2/Consortium layer via separate message binding (not EIP-712). Confidence medium — domain separator not directly inspected but OZ standard implementation is well-established.

Lombard uses TransparentUpgradeableProxy pattern (not UUPS) for all proxy contracts: LBTC, Consortium, BridgeV2. With Transparent proxy, the upgrade path is via the ProxyAdmin calling upgradeToAndCall() — there is no _authorizeUpgrade() function to protect. The UUPS authorization check factor is N/A for Transparent proxy pattern.

All examined implementation contracts properly protect initialize(): (1) Consortium.sol — constructor() { _disableInitializers(); } AND function initialize(address _owner) external initializer; (2) BridgeV2.sol — constructor() { _disableInitializers(); } AND function initialize(address owner_, IMailbox mailbox_) external initializer; (3) NativeLBTC.sol — constructor() { _disableInitializers(); } AND function initialize(...) external initializer; (4) StakedLBTC.sol — constructor() { _disableInitializers(); } AND function initialize(address treasury, address initialOwner, uint48 initialOwnerDelay) external initializer. BasculeV2.sol uses a standard constructor (non-proxied) — no initialize() function, N/A for that contract. No unprotected initialize() found across reviewed contracts.

_disableInitializers() confirmed present in constructors of all proxied implementation contracts: Consortium.sol, BridgeV2.sol, NativeLBTC.sol, StakedLBTC.sol. BasculeV2.sol uses standard constructor (not proxied) — N/A for that contract. Not confirmed for all peripheral contracts (PMM, factory, StakeAndBake) but core proxied contracts all comply. Confidence high for core contracts.

14+ audit engagements across 7 firms covering every major contract module: V1 core (Halborn 13-day, Veridise 9-day), V2 full stack (OZ 32-day Golang+EVM, Veridise 65-day EVM only, Halborn V2), Yield Bearing (OZ + Sherlock), StakeAndBake (ABDK), BridgeV2/BTC.b (OZ), Multipauser (OZ + Sherlock). Each successive audit targeted a specific feature set rather than the entire codebase, keeping scope focused and audit depth appropriate. OZ V2 at 32 days covering the most complex release (39 findings identified) demonstrates adequate depth. No indication of audit-complexity ratio exceeding reasonable bounds.

Current Lombard documentation states that critical operations require signatures from at least 10 of 14 Consortium members. It does not publish an on-chain mapping from that policy to the reviewed upgrade-admin contracts or identify each role holder, so effective upgrade custody cannot be verified from the available public documentation.

Lombard documents a 10-of-14 threshold for critical Consortium operations. The documentation does not establish that a particular Safe is the current upgrade authority, so an upgrade-multisig M/N configuration and its adequacy cannot be independently assessed.

The public documentation describes a 10-of-14 Consortium approval policy for critical operations, but does not publish a complete current on-chain role map for production admin paths. A single-admin EOA path therefore cannot be confirmed or ruled out from the available public evidence.

The available current public documentation does not establish an upgrade Safe, its signer threshold, or its relationship to the production admin path. Low-threshold upgrade-multisig exposure cannot be independently assessed.
The available current public documentation does not identify the signers for the production upgrade authority. Signer co-hosting cannot be independently assessed.
The available current public documentation does not identify the signers for the production upgrade authority. Hot-wallet signing posture cannot be independently assessed.
factor_scores.notes: No current public source identifies the production upgrade signers or their hot-wallet posture; revisit if Lombard publishes a role map.

factor_scores.evidence_summary: The available current public documentation does not identify the production upgrade signer set or its change history. Signer rotation recency cannot be independently assessed.

Lombard's current documentation describes the Consortium threshold for critical operations but does not publish a current on-chain upgrade timelock address or minimum delay. The duration applicable to upgrades is therefore not independently established.

The available current documentation does not map sensitive production actions to an on-chain timelock or state which actions, if any, bypass it. Timelock coverage cannot be assessed from public documentation alone.

Current public documentation does not identify the holders of pause and upgrade authority or demonstrate that they are distinct. Role separation is not independently verifiable from the available evidence.
Current public documentation does not publish a complete current assignment of upgrade, fee, and oracle administration roles. Separation of those authorities cannot be independently assessed.

Lombard documents 10-of-14 signatures for critical Consortium operations and separately discloses that governance characteristics may evolve. It does not provide sufficient current public evidence to determine whether any token-voting execution path is live and flash-loanable.

Lombard documents a 10-of-14 Consortium threshold for critical operations, but the available public documentation does not establish the full current set of governance execution paths. Whether any quorum can be obtained through borrowed token voting is not independently assessable.
The available current documentation does not identify a proposal execution mechanism or publish its delay. A sub-24-hour proposal-execution delay cannot be confirmed.
The public materials reviewed do not publish a current on-chain proposal executor, its target restrictions, or an equivalent role map. Arbitrary proposal execution cannot be assessed.
Current public documentation does not identify a dedicated emergency-veto mechanism or its on-chain authority. The presence and independence of a veto control cannot be assessed.
The public materials reviewed do not establish the current access control or timelock status of rescue functions. Whether a rescue path can bypass a timelock cannot be independently assessed.

Lombard documents that critical operations require signatures from at least 10 of 14 Consortium members. It does not publish the current on-chain mint authority, any supply cap, or a contract-to-Consortium role binding, so unlimited admin minting cannot be independently assessed.
The current public documentation does not identify the current production admin, deployer, or role-transfer history. A continuing deployer-admin relationship cannot be confirmed or ruled out.
Because the current public documentation does not identify the production admin wallet or provide a complete role map, the relevant administrator's exposure to flagged addresses cannot be assessed.

The public materials reviewed do not publish a current proposal-to-deployment process or proposal payloads. Constructor-argument consistency against governance approval cannot be independently assessed.

The available current public documentation does not provide a complete, versioned inventory linking every production contract in scope to verified explorer source. The absence of unverified production contracts cannot be independently assessed.

Lombard's current documentation identifies 14 independent institutional Consortium members and requires at least 10 signatures for critical operations. It does not map the named institutions to current on-chain signing keys or provide a token-holder distribution suitable for a Gini calculation. Governance concentration is therefore only partially transparent.

Lombard documents Chainlink and RedStone price/Proof-of-Reserve infrastructure across supported networks, including its own EVM PoR contract and RedStone PoR contracts. The LBTC fundamental rate is an on-chain consortium-authorized exchange-rate oracle. The documented provider set is not a spot-DEX oracle path. Green: the public provider and contract documentation identifies established, independently verifiable oracle infrastructure.

Lombard publicly lists Chainlink and RedStone oracle/PoR deployments, but does not publicly designate a primary, secondary, or fallback order for each price feed. The StakedLBTCOracle accepts a consortium-proof-authorized exchange-rate update and its reviewed code exposes no secondary oracle. Yellow: provider roles and failover ordering are not fully disclosed.

Public documentation identifies direct dependencies on Babylon for Bitcoin staking; Cubist's CubeSigner and Bascule verification layer for key management and independent deposit/redemption checks; Chainlink CCIP for EVM/Solana bridge infrastructure; IBC for Cosmos routes; oracle/data providers; and relayer infrastructure. Failure of Babylon, Bascule/CubeSigner, a bridge provider, or relayer can impair staking, mint/redeem, transfer, or price-data functions. Yellow: several critical dependency classes remain externally operated, with Bascule operated by Cubist.

The StakedLBTCOracle submits a ratio only after Consortium proof verification and exposes no secondary-oracle or last-known-price fallback in the reviewed source. Lombard documents PoR attestation updates every 10 minutes, but does not disclose a stale-feed fallback policy. Yellow: failure behavior is therefore revert/no declared fallback rather than a documented graceful-degradation path.

Babylon unavailability can impair Bitcoin staking and yield operations. Bascule or CubeSigner disruption can impair the independent verification/key-management stages required for minting, redemption, and payouts. A CCIP, IBC, relayer, or oracle/provider failure can delay or prevent the affected cross-chain or price-data function. Lombard documents dual verification for bridge transfers and a Bascule second check for mint/redemption flows, but its risk disclosure confirms that third-party failures can cause service disruption or asset loss. Yellow: material failure modes and mitigations are documented, while several dependencies remain external.

[★ CRITICAL — GREEN] No DEX spot price oracle found in any Lombard source file. LBTC minting/burning is Consortium-authorized, not price-oracle gated. BTC/USD from Chainlink is a push oracle with no DEX component. StakedLBTCOracle derives LBTC/BTC exchange rate from Consortium-signed ratio, not DEX. No slot0(), getReserves(), or equivalent DEX price read found in contracts/LBTC/, contracts/PoR/, or contracts/bridge/ directories. Source inspection of all oracle-related contract directories confirms absence of any spot DEX oracle dependency.

N/A — Lombard Finance does not use DEX TWAP oracles. Source inspection of all oracle-related contracts found no OracleLibrary.consult() or equivalent TWAP call. All price feeds are Chainlink/RedStone push oracles. Factor does not apply to this protocol type.
N/A — Lombard Finance does not use DEX pool oracles. No pool TVL measurement required. Source inspection confirms Chainlink/RedStone push oracles only. Factor does not apply to this protocol type.

Lombard does not use DEX pool oracle; single-pool oracle concern does not apply. For Chainlink BTC/USD (0xF4030086522a5bEEa4988F8cA5B36dbC97BeE88c): multi-source aggregation is inherent to Chainlink's AggregatorV3 design (multiple independent node operators; medianized). Not a single-pool oracle. No DEX oracle of any kind found in Lombard source. Green: Chainlink's multi-node aggregation design inherently meets the no-single-pool criterion.

StakedLBTCOracle validates each rate update against a ratio-change threshold and reverts TooBigRatioChange when the permitted interval-adjusted deviation is exceeded. No general cross-oracle price-deviation breaker was identified in the reviewed Lombard source. Yellow: the LBTC-rate control is present, while broader price-feed circuit breaking is not publicly established.

StakedLBTCOracle initializes ratioThreshold to 0.1% and computes the permitted ratio change from that threshold and the switch interval. That 10-bps default is well below the rubric's 2,000-bps green bound. Green: the documented on-chain LBTC-rate deviation limit is conservative.

The reviewed StakedLBTCOracle exposes a switch-time model for the current or previous ratio but no explicit maximum-age rejection for stale oracle data. Lombard documents ten-minute PoR publication cadence, not a contract-enforced stale-read threshold. Yellow: an explicit updatedAt/maxStaleness guard was not established.

Lombard documents a Chainlink price-feed deployment but the reviewed public materials do not establish the bound configuration of the underlying Chainlink aggregator for the relevant feed. Gray: minAnswer/maxAnswer configuration could not be independently verified from the public evidence reviewed.

Lombard does not use LP token balanceOf for pricing. LBTC/BTC exchange rate is derived from Consortium-published ratio via StakedLBTCOracle. No balanceOf call found in any price calculation path in the LBTC/ directory or oracle contracts. Donation-manipulation via LP token balanceOf is not applicable to this protocol's price mechanism.

Bascule is an independent verification layer operated by Cubist and must validate deposits before minting; its failure can therefore impair the mint path. Lombard's documentation also identifies trustless relayer infrastructure, while CCIP uses independent node operators and a Risk Management Network. Yellow: the public architecture still identifies a material single-operator Bascule dependency, with no public failover arrangement established.

Bridge surface confirmed. Lombard documents a dual-verification bridge architecture: Chainlink CCIP is the external bridge for EVM-compatible chains and Solana, IBC serves Cosmos routes, and a native Consortium bridge is used for select routes. Bridge transfers are therefore in scope for category 10.

Lombard publicly documents 14 independent institutional Consortium members and a 10-of-14 cryptographic threshold for critical operations. The native bridge relies on that Consortium; CCIP also supplies its own independent bridge validation. Fourteen signers satisfies the rubric's green validator-count band.

The documented Consortium threshold is 10-of-14, a two-thirds supermajority. The public verifier stores a weighted validator set and rejects a proof below its weight threshold. CCIP bridge transfers require an independent CCIP approval plus Consortium co-signature. Green: the native bridge threshold exceeds a simple majority.

The 14 documented Consortium members span crypto institutions, market makers, mining pools, institutional validators, and security/research firms. This supports organizational diversity, but no public ASN, datacenter, or signer-custodian inventory establishes infrastructure separation. Yellow: co-hosting cannot be independently ruled out from public evidence.

[CRITICAL — GREEN] The native bridge Consortium verifier uses OpenZeppelin ECDSA.tryRecover and explicitly continues unless RecoverError.NoError is returned; a recovered address must also match the configured validator. The reviewed native bridge code contains no raw unchecked ecrecover result. Lombard documents CCIP as the external bridge validation layer. No unchecked zero-address recovery was found in the native verifier.

Mailbox/GMP path: inbound messages validated against $.inboundMessagePath[payload.msgPath] which encodes remote mailbox + chain; srcChainId is implicitly bound via path ID (path-based srcChainId binding). BridgeV2: chainId extracted via $.mailbox.getInboundMessagePath(payload.msgPath); rate limits keyed by (sourceChain, token) pair. CCIP path: sourceChainSelector is native to Chainlink's Any2EVMMessage struct; received by Lombard's TokenPool via CCIP's structured message format. All three active bridge paths bind messages to their source chain identifier.

BridgeV2: payloadSpent[payload.id] mapping prevents double-spend; reverts with BridgeV2_PayloadSpent() on replay attempt. Mailbox: deliveredPayload[payloadHash] mapping prevents re-delivery of the same payload. CCIP: Chainlink's own sequence number infrastructure handles replay prevention at the protocol layer independently of Lombard's source. All active bridge paths implement replay protection through payload-hash or sequence tracking.

[CRITICAL — GREEN] The native BridgeV2 rejects zero chain IDs, token identifiers, bridge paths, senders, and recipients at configuration and message-processing boundaries. Mailbox rejects zero chain/mailbox values when paths are enabled and zero recipients on sends. Inbound messages are admitted through enabled paths and Consortium proof verification; no default bytes32(0) proof root was found accepted as valid in the reviewed native bridge path.

Yellow: the shared key-management dependency warrants caution, but the >30% key-custody threshold is not publicly verifiable.
